title: Document Model
description: Model nested document facts with explicit validation, identity, embedding and reference choices, and missing-value semantics, with MySQL JSON practice kept distinct from native document-engine verification.
notes:
## Storing a structured aggregate as a document

The document data model represents information through documents that can contain named fields, nested objects, and arrays. JSON-like examples make the structure readable, while actual products may use a representation such as BSON with additional supported types. A document is more than an opaque string when the database can interpret supported internal fields for queries and indexes.

MongoDB is a familiar document database, but the model is not defined by one product's exact API or transaction limits. MySQL also provides JSON facilities inside a relational database. Using a JSON column does not turn every surrounding table and operation into a standalone document database, and equivalent-looking JSON does not prove identical behavior across engines.

Consider a learning catalog document with a title, level, and author object. Another document can contain an optional estimated duration. The representation can support variation, but the application still needs a contract for which fields are required, what types they accept, and how readers interpret absent values.

## Keeping flexibility separate from missing rules

Flexible schema means documents can have different shapes under the selected product's rules. It does not mean structure is irrelevant or validation is impossible. MongoDB supports schema validation, including field-type and value restrictions. A product can reject invalid writes or use other configured behavior, so inspect the actual validation policy rather than assuming all collections accept everything.

The phrase schema-on-read emphasizes interpreting structure when reading, but many real designs combine reader expectations with write-time validation. A title can be required while an optional duration remains flexible. Without a shared contract, one writer might store duration as an integer number of minutes and another as a sentence, making later filtering ambiguous.

A migration from one document shape to another also needs compatibility planning. Adding an optional field differs from replacing a string field with an object. Existing documents and older readers may remain in the system. A schema-free slogan does not supply an evolution policy or make every change invisible.

## Preserving document identity

A document needs an identity appropriate to the application's references and updates. Two catalog entries can share the title SQL Basics without representing the same course. A stable identifier distinguishes them even when their visible fields match. Updating a title should not accidentally replace the identity used by bookmarks, enrollment records, or external links.

Embedded values need their own identity decisions. An address value might simply be part of one user's current profile, while an independently managed delivery location may require a distinct identity and lifecycle. A nested object does not automatically become an independently identified entity merely because it has several named fields.

Arrays introduce another distinction: an array position is not always a stable identifier for an entry. Reordering or inserting elements can change positions. If callers must update one address across time, a modeled entry identifier can be more appropriate than assuming the third array item always refers to the same location.

## Choosing embedding from the facts

Embedding places related data inside the parent document. A user's addresses array can make retrieving that defined aggregate convenient. This differs from storing each address in a separate relation or collection and connecting it by references. The choice should follow ownership, access patterns, update frequency, size, and integrity requirements.

Embedding an exclusively owned value does not necessarily create redundant copies of the same fact. Redundancy becomes a separate concern when an authoritative address or course fact is duplicated across documents. If one fact has several copies, updating only one can leave readers with conflicting states. The design needs an explicit source-of-truth and propagation policy.

Do not call every nested array automatically a normalization defect. Ask what each value represents and whether it is intentionally part of an aggregate or a separately shared fact. A document layout can be appropriate for one task while awkward for another that needs cross-entry uniqueness, independent history, or frequent updates to a shared entity.

## Understanding document queries and indexes

A document engine can offer predicates and indexes over supported fields within documents. That distinguishes its rich document interface from the simplest opaque-value key-value abstraction. Real products overlap: some key-value systems also offer structured values and secondary indexes. Classify the actual access contract rather than drawing a universal boundary from one marketing category.

A query for beginner catalog entries must define how missing level values and unexpected types behave. An index can help supported predicates, but it does not establish field validity or actor permission. A query that executes successfully can still expose an unrelated document population or interpret mixed value types incorrectly.

Read costs depend on the actual query, index, document size, and engine. Fetching one useful aggregate can avoid assembling separate facts, but very large documents or duplicated data can create other costs. Fewer visible joins is not a universal performance proof. Measure the workload and preserve required consistency and access behavior.

## Distinguishing missing fields and null values

A missing field and a field explicitly containing JSON null are different document states. An empty string is different again, as is the string whose four letters spell null. A reader should preserve distinctions the task needs instead of replacing every case with the same blank label.

In MySQL, JSON_CONTAINS_PATH can check whether a path exists, JSON_EXTRACT obtains a supported path value, and JSON_TYPE can distinguish an explicit JSON null from a string value. JSON_UNQUOTE can expose a selected JSON string as text. These are MySQL-oriented examples, not MongoDB query syntax.

```sql
SELECT document_id,
       JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(body, '$.title')) AS title
FROM catalog_documents
WHERE JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(body, '$.level')) = 'beginner'
ORDER BY document_id;
```

The fixture defines level as a string when present. A document lacking that level does not qualify through the equality condition. The task also requires a title for qualifying fixtures; simply using a valid JSON type does not enforce that application-level rule. Syntactic JSON validity and schema validity are different checks.

## Defining update and transaction boundaries

A document can be a useful update boundary when related values change together through a supported operation. That does not mean every document store is limited to one-document transactions or that every multi-document workflow is automatically atomic. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on supported deployments, with specific version and operational requirements.

The right boundary follows the business operation. Updating duplicated course facts across several documents requires a consistency policy even when each individual update is atomic. An interrupted propagation can leave mixed versions. References, embedding, transactions, or a reviewed asynchronous mechanism each carry trade-offs rather than removing the requirement to define consistency.

A client retrieving a document also needs trusted authorization for its fields and records. Hiding a nested field in the interface is not enough if the response still contains it. Flexible structure must not become a shortcut for storing secrets or exposing private profile data inside a convenient aggregate.

## Comparing document and wide-column organization

Document and wide-column models organize information differently. Documents emphasize structured values and aggregates; wide-column systems commonly emphasize keyed partitions and named column organization under their actual product rules. Cassandra and Bigtable are not identical products, and neither category supplies a universal write-throughput guarantee.

An event dataset might fit several representations. The choice depends on query population, access keys, retention, update patterns, and transaction needs. Compare those concrete properties rather than assuming deeply nested data always requires a document store or that high volume always requires a particular NoSQL category.

A MySQL JSON exercise can test document-field reasoning without proving native MongoDB behavior. Likewise, MariaDB compatibility execution does not establish every MySQL JSON storage or indexing guarantee. Record the engine and the exact functions exercised, and keep native and provider verification separate.

## Reviewing a document contract

Use original fixtures covering optional fields, explicit null, empty text, repeated labels, and nested values. Verify required fields and types where the actual engine enforces them, then inspect query meaning and output population separately. A valid JSON parser result cannot substitute for authorization or business-schema checks.

The document model is useful when an aggregate structure matches required facts and access patterns. Preserve identity, define absence and validation policies, and make embedding or references deliberate. That produces understandable documents without claiming that flexibility removes schemas, that nesting guarantees performance, or that a successful field query verifies every native engine feature.

questions.question_text: What is the defining storage unit of the document model?
options: A fixed-schema table row
A self-contained, semi-structured document (e.g., JSON/BSON) that can nest objects and arrays
An opaque binary blob addressable only by key
A wide sparse column family
questions.explanation: Document databases store data as self-contained documents, typically JSON or BSON, which can include nested objects and arrays.

questions.question_text: What does flexible document structure imply about validation?
options: The schema is enforced strictly at write time by the database
Documents can vary, while configured write validation and reader contracts can still impose rules
Every document must be validated against a fixed schema before insertion
Reads are not permitted until a schema is defined
questions.explanation: Flexible does not mean unvalidated or without a shared schema.

questions.question_text: Which of these databases is a well-known document-model implementation?
options: MongoDB
Redis
Cassandra
Neo4j
questions.explanation: MongoDB is one of the most widely used document databases, storing data as BSON documents.

questions.question_text: Which capability distinguishes rich document access from the simplest opaque-value key-value abstraction?
options: Whether the database uses a network connection
Querying supported internal fields, while real product capabilities can overlap
Whether the database supports replication
Whether the database is open source
questions.explanation: This is not a universal classification test for every modern product.

questions.question_text: How should an embedded addresses array be evaluated against separate address facts?
options: Because arrays are not allowed in relational databases
Review aggregate ownership, shared identity, access patterns, and whether authoritative facts are duplicated
Because the document has no _id field
Because JSON cannot represent arrays
questions.explanation: Embedding is not automatically redundant duplication or a universal normalization violation.

questions.question_text: What is a key trade-off of embedding denormalized data (like duplicated address info) across many documents?
options: There are no trade-offs; it is strictly better
Updating a piece of duplicated data requires updating every document copy, risking inconsistency
It makes single-document reads slower
It requires a JOIN operation for every query
questions.explanation: Because data is duplicated across documents rather than normalized once, updates must be propagated to every copy, which can introduce inconsistency if missed.

questions.question_text: How should document and wide-column models be compared?
options: They are functionally identical
Compare actual structure and access contracts rather than assuming a universal performance ranking
Column-family databases cannot store more than one row
Document databases cannot be distributed across servers
questions.explanation: Cassandra and other products have specific schema and consistency behavior.

questions.question_text: Can MongoDB support multi-document transactions on suitable deployments?
options: Yes, under the supported deployment, version, and operational rules
Support for SQL joins across collections
Automatic schema enforcement
Elimination of the _id field
questions.explanation: The model does not imply single-document-only transactions or universal support in every environment.

questions.question_text: Does valid JSON alone prove a required title field exists?
options: Yes; JSON requires every title
No; syntactic validity and application schema are separate
Only if the value is stored in a table
Only if the document is short
questions.explanation: Required field rules need explicit validation.

questions.question_text: What can make an array position unsuitable as a durable address identity?
options: Every array is unordered in all engines
Positions automatically grant permissions
Insertion and reordering can change positions
Every address is a database role
questions.explanation: A stable entry reference may need its own identifier.

questions.question_text: Two documents share title SQL Basics but have distinct IDs. What should a bookmark preserve?
options: Only the title by assumption
Only its current array position
The intended stable document identity
Only the document length
questions.explanation: Equal labels do not identify the same entity.

questions.question_text: An exclusively owned address is embedded once in one profile. Is duplicated authority inevitable?
options: Yes; every nested value has many copies
Only if the city is long
Only if the document has an ID
No; assess whether any fact is actually copied elsewhere
questions.explanation: Embedding and redundant duplication are distinct design questions.

questions.question_text: A city path is absent in one document and explicitly JSON null in another. What should review recognize?
options: Two different document states
One identical mandatory value
Two SQL primary keys
A guaranteed syntax error
questions.explanation: A missing path differs from an existing path holding JSON null.

questions.question_text: A city is the JSON string null. Is it the same as JSON null?
options: Yes; four letters always mean absence
No; the string is a recorded text value
Only if JSON_UNQUOTE is used
Only if the field is indexed
questions.explanation: The JSON type distinguishes string content from null.

questions.question_text: A required level predicate compares to beginner, but the path is missing. Does the fixture equality select it?
options: Yes; missing means beginner
Only if the title repeats
No
Only if the document is stored last
questions.explanation: The missing extracted value does not satisfy the stated equality.

questions.question_text: One authoritative course title is copied into many documents and only one copy changes. What must the design address?
options: Only the indentation
Only the object ID type
Only the document display color
Consistency and propagation of the shared fact
questions.explanation: Redundant authoritative copies can diverge.

questions.question_text: A document update is atomic. Does that alone make a multi-document workflow atomic?
options: No; the full operation needs supported guarantees
Yes; every document store groups all writes
Only if all titles match
Only if there are two documents
questions.explanation: The workflow boundary can extend beyond one document.

questions.question_text: A browser hides a private nested field but still receives it. What remains wrong?
options: The field was securely deleted
The response exposed data beyond the intended presentation
The database necessarily has no schema
The JSON parser guarantees secrecy
questions.explanation: UI hiding is not a trusted data-exposure boundary.

questions.question_text: A MySQL JSON mirror passes on MariaDB. What remains separate?
options: The observed compatibility output
The fixture data used
Exact MySQL/provider and native MongoDB behavior
The functions executed in that run
questions.explanation: Execution evidence is scoped to the actual engine and operation.

questions.question_text: A small embedded read is fast. What should not be inferred without broader evidence?
options: That the measured read completed
That structure can influence cost
That the workload has an access pattern
Every embedding and update pattern is superior
questions.explanation: Model performance is workload-specific.

coding_problems.title: Read a field-filtered JSON catalog
coding_problems.task: Return document_id and title for JSON catalog documents with level equal to the string beginner. Extract title as unquoted text and order by document_id. Qualifying fixture documents always have a string title. This is MySQL JSON practice, not MongoDB query execution.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE catalog_documents (document_id INT PRIMARY KEY, body JSON NOT NULL);
constraints: level and title are strings when provided in these fixtures
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT document_id,JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(body,'$.title')) AS title FROM catalog_documents WHERE JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(body,'$.level'))='beginner' ORDER BY document_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The path predicate defines the intended document population and the projection preserves the explicit identity and text title.

coding_problems.title: Distinguish absent paths, JSON null, and text
coding_problems.task: For every catalog_documents row, interpret $.address.city and return document_id, city_status, city_value. Status is missing for an absent path, json_null for explicit JSON null, and text for a string (including an empty string or the letters null). city_value is the unquoted text for text status and SQL NULL otherwise. Order by document_id. Fixtures contain only these three city states.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE catalog_documents (document_id INT PRIMARY KEY, body JSON NOT NULL);
coding_problems.expected:
document_id	city_status	city_value
1	missing	NULL
2	json_null	NULL
3	text	Pune
4	text	null
5	text
constraints: Only absent, JSON null, or string city values appear
Do not replace missing values with empty text
The status column preserves the distinction
edge_cases: A missing address also means absent city path
Explicit JSON null differs from the string null
An empty recorded city is text
hints: Convert explicit null to SQL NULL deliberately
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT document_id,CASE WHEN JSON_CONTAINS_PATH(body,'one','$.address.city')=0 THEN 'missing' WHEN JSON_TYPE(JSON_EXTRACT(body,'$.address.city'))='NULL' THEN 'json_null' ELSE 'text' END AS city_status,CASE WHEN JSON_TYPE(JSON_EXTRACT(body,'$.address.city'))='STRING' THEN JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(body,'$.address.city')) ELSE NULL END AS city_value FROM catalog_documents ORDER BY document_id;
coding_problems.explanation: Existence and JSON type checks keep absent paths separate from explicit null and recorded text. The result maps only the defined absence states to SQL NULL.

validation_cases.expected:
document_id	city_status	city_value
7	missing	NULL
8	text	NULL

original_questions.question_text: What is the defining storage unit of the document model?
options: A fixed-schema table row
A self-contained, semi-structured document (e.g., JSON/BSON) that can nest objects and arrays
An opaque binary blob addressable only by key
A wide sparse column family
original_questions.explanation: Document databases store data as self-contained documents, typically JSON or BSON, which can include nested objects and arrays.

original_questions.question_text: What does 'schema-on-read' mean in the context of document databases?
options: The schema is enforced strictly at write time by the database
Documents in the same collection are not required to share an identical structure; the application interprets structure when reading
Every document must be validated against a fixed schema before insertion
Reads are not permitted until a schema is defined
original_questions.explanation: Schema-on-read means the database does not enforce a rigid structure at write time; different documents in a collection can have different shapes, with structure interpreted at read/query time.

original_questions.question_text: Which of these databases is a well-known document-model implementation?
options: MongoDB
Redis
Cassandra
Neo4j
original_questions.explanation: MongoDB is one of the most widely used document databases, storing data as BSON documents.

original_questions.question_text: What is the clearest distinguishing test between a document database and a key-value store?
options: Whether the database uses a network connection
Whether the database can query and index fields inside the stored value, not just retrieve it whole by key
Whether the database supports replication
Whether the database is open source
original_questions.explanation: A key-value store treats its value as an opaque blob; a document store understands and can query the internal structure of the document.

original_questions.question_text: In the example user document with an embedded 'addresses' array, why is this considered denormalization compared to a relational design?
options: Because arrays are not allowed in relational databases
Because data that would normally be split into a separate 'addresses' table is embedded directly inside the parent document
Because the document has no _id field
Because JSON cannot represent arrays
original_questions.explanation: In a relational design, addresses would typically live in a separate normalized table joined by a foreign key; the document model embeds them directly in the same document.

original_questions.question_text: What is a key trade-off of embedding denormalized data (like duplicated address info) across many documents?
options: There are no trade-offs; it is strictly better
Updating a piece of duplicated data requires updating every document copy, risking inconsistency
It makes single-document reads slower
It requires a JOIN operation for every query
original_questions.explanation: Because data is duplicated across documents rather than normalized once, updates must be propagated to every copy, which can introduce inconsistency if missed.

original_questions.question_text: How does a document database differ from a column-family database like Cassandra?
options: They are functionally identical
Document stores optimize for flexible, deeply nested JSON-like data, while column-family stores organize sparse columns grouped into families optimized for very high write throughput at massive scale
Column-family databases cannot store more than one row
Document databases cannot be distributed across servers
original_questions.explanation: Column-family stores like Cassandra structure data around static column families for extreme write scalability, whereas document stores focus on flexible nested structures resembling application objects.

original_questions.question_text: As of MongoDB 4.0+, what transactional capability was added beyond the model's natural single-document atomicity?
options: Multi-document ACID transactions
Support for SQL joins across collections
Automatic schema enforcement
Elimination of the _id field
original_questions.explanation: MongoDB introduced multi-document ACID transactions starting in version 4.0, though single-document atomicity remains the model's natural strength.

diagrams.description: The path may be absent, explicitly null, or a recorded string. The exercise keeps a separate status so even the text NULL can be distinguished from an SQL-null output value.
